stories.title: SIOR Fall Event Combines Networking, Examining the Industry’s Future
stories.excerpt: The Society of Industrial and Office REALTORS (SIOR) concluded its 2026 Fall Event in New York City after bringing together more than 1,200 commercial real estate professionals from 21 countries for four days of networking, professional development and discussions on the forces shaping the industry’s future. Held Oct. 19–22 at the New York Hilton Midtown, the event marked a milestone in SIOR’s 85th anniversary year, celebrating the organization’s longstanding commitment to professional excellence, trusted relationships and global collaboration. The conference featured keynote presentations from former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, Moody’s Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi, bestselling author and leadership expert Caroline Webb, and legendary New York commercial real estate broker Bob Knakal, alongside educational sessions examining emerging opportunities and challenges across the industry. “Our Fall Event in New York was a tremendous success, bringing together commercial real estate professionals from around the world to exchange ideas, strengthen relationships and discuss the opportunities and challenges shaping our industry,” said David C. Lockwood III, SIOR, CEO of SIOR. “As we celebrate our 85th anniversary, this gathering reinforced what has made SIOR such an enduring organization: a global community of professionals committed to excellence, collaboration and helping one another succeed. Those values have guided us for eight decades and will continue to drive our growth and impact in the years ahead.” A central theme throughout the conference was the growing importance of specialized expertise, trusted relationships and adaptability as commercial real estate professionals navigate changing economic conditions, technology and occupier demands. Pictured: SIOR CEO David C. Lockwood III. The post SIOR Fall Event Combines Networking, Examining the Industry’s Future appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: The Society of Industrial and Office REALTORS held its 2026 Fall Event in New York City, drawing over 1,200 commercial real estate professionals from 21 countries for networking and professional development. The four-day conference featured keynotes from Moody's Analytics chief economist Mark Zandi, former Gov. Chris Christie, leadership expert Caroline Webb, and prominent NYC broker Bob Knakal, alongside sessions on industry opportunities and challenges. The event celebrated SIOR's 85th anniversary and its commitment to professional excellence and global collaboration.
stories.impact: Limited direct relevance to multifamily development. The gathering signals macro-sentiment among CRE professionals but does not surface specific demand signals, financing conditions, or supply pipeline data that would shape apartment acquisition or development decisions.

stories.title: Barings Acquires Ralphs-Anchored Center from First Washington
stories.excerpt: CBRE arranged the $66.2-million sale of Village Center at Rose, a 118,876-square-foot, Ralphs-anchored shopping center at 600-858 N. Rose Dr. in Placentia. Barings acquired the fully leased property from First Washington Realty. Jimmy Slusher, Mark Damiani, James Tyrrell and Shaya McClanahan of CBRE’s National Retail Partners – West represented the seller. Built in 1996, Village Center at Rose sits on 10.15 acres at the northeast corner of North Rose Drive and Alta Vista Street. Ralphs, which has operated at the center since it opened, occupies 37% of the gross leasable area. Eighty percent of existing tenants have occupied the property for more than 10 years. “The center serves a dense trade area with strong household incomes and limited new retail supply,” Damiani said. “More than 147,000 people live within three miles of the center, and nearby new housing continues to add to the demand that Ralphs and the surrounding tenants serve.” The post Barings Acquires Ralphs-Anchored Center from First Washington appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: Barings purchased Village Center at Rose, a fully leased 118,876-square-foot shopping center in Placentia, California, for $66.2 million ($557/SF). Built in 1996, the property is anchored by Ralphs supermarket and sits on 10.15 acres in a supply-constrained trade area. The deal highlights strong household incomes and ongoing housing demand in the dense Orange County submarket where 147,000+ people live within a three-mile radius.
stories.impact: The sale signals institutional capital confidence in necessity-based retail in supply-constrained Orange County—a proxy for durable household formation and income stability in the region. The buyer's explicit emphasis on 'supply-constrained market' and 10+ year tenant tenure underscores tight retail real estate. For multifamily developers in Orange County submarkets (Placentia, Anaheim, Santa Ana), this validates strong demographic fundamentals and stable household economics that support apartment demand and rent resilience; density and limited new supply make infill/mixed-use residential development sites more valuable.

stories.title: Madison Realty Lends $463M for First St. Regis Condo in Sunny Isles, Fla.
stories.excerpt: Fortune International Group and Château Group have secured a $463 million construction debt package from Madison Realty Capital to complete the St. Regis Residences condo development in Sunny Isles Beach, Fla. The oceanfront project at 18801 Collins Avenue will include two 62-story skyscrapers. The debt package will refinance the existing debt from Bank OZK, which has issued $418 million for the development since 2024, and provide the financing to complete the construction of the so-called South Tower, which broke ground in 2023. The 170-unit skyscraper is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, according to a representative for the sponsors. So far, 80 percent of units have presold, generating over $1.6 billion. Construction has yet to start for the 150-unit North Tower, though it did secure $114 million in financing from City National Bank of Florida earlier this year. Berkadia’s Scott Wadler, Michael Basinski, Mitch Sinberg, Matt Robbins, Brad Williamson and Matthew Monahemi arranged the recent financing from New York-based Madison Realty Capital. “This transaction reflects our conviction in the Sunny Isles Beach submarket,” Josh Zegen, co-founder and managing principal of Madison Realty Capital, said in a statement. “Demand at the top of the market is increasingly concentrated in projects that pair oceanfront scarcity with the service and amenities of a five-star hotel.” Last year, the lender supplied $630 million for Gil Dezer to finish the Bentley-branded, oceanfront condo skyscraper nearby. The construction debt was South Florida’s largest loan issued for a luxury condo in 2026. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.

stories.summary: Fortune International Group and Château Group secured a $463 million construction financing package from Madison Realty Capital to complete the St. Regis Residences oceanfront condo development in Sunny Isles Beach, Florida. The refinance replaces and expands Bank OZK's $418 million facility. The South Tower (170 units) is expected to complete by end of 2028 with 80% presales generating over $1.6 billion; the North Tower (150 units) has not yet begun construction.
stories.impact: Condo construction financing availability and 80% presale velocity signal strong Miami-Dade luxury residential demand and investor appetite. However, this is a for-sale condo project, not rental multifamily. For multifamily developers in South Florida, the deal underscores: (1) capital is flowing to residential in Miami-Dade, reducing financing competition with rental players; (2) luxury presale absorption at high price points validates strong high-income in-migration; (3) but extended build timelines (through 2028) and delayed North Tower commencement suggest capital is selective—rental developers must show strong fundamentals and seasoned sponsors to access comparable financing in the Miami market.

stories.title: JLL Arranges Financing for Lightstone Acquisition on Upper West Side
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets arranged acquisition financing for Lightstone’s purchase of 323 W. 96th St., a 174-unit multifamily property on Manhattan’s Upper West Side. Senior managing director Peter Rotchford and managing director Michael Shmuely worked on behalf of Lightstone to secure the financing from MF1, a wholly owned subsidiary of Berkshire Residential Investments. Lightstone is acquiring the property from Pinnacle Group for a reported $88 million. Located between Riverside Park and West End Avenue, 323 W. 96th is a 15-story, 174-unit rental building. The 136,651 square-foot property was built in 2004. “323 W. 96th St. is a well-located asset with strong existing demand, an experienced sponsor and a clear business plan for creating additional value,” said Rotchford. “There continues to be significant lender appetite for high-quality multifamily opportunities, particularly in supply-constrained New York City neighborhoods. MF1 understood both the strength of the Upper West Side fundamentals and Lightstone’s plan for the property, allowing us to structure financing that supports the acquisition and Lightstone’s investment in the asset.” The post JLL Arranges Financing for Lightstone Acquisition on Upper West Side appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: Lightstone purchased 323 W. 96th Street, a 174-unit multifamily rental building on Manhattan's Upper West Side, for $88 million from Pinnacle Group. The 15-story property built in 2004 is located between Riverside Park and West End Avenue. MF1, a subsidiary of Berkshire Residential Investments, provided acquisition financing, with lender commentary highlighting significant institutional appetite for high-quality multifamily in supply-constrained New York City neighborhoods.
stories.impact: The deal and lender's statement validate sustained institutional capital appetite for stabilized multifamily in Manhattan's constrained supply markets, particularly UWS. For Trammell Crow and peer developers, this signals: (1) acquisitions of value-add rental buildings in prime NYC submarkets remain well-capitalized; (2) supply constraints in the UWS—one of Manhattan's tightest rental markets—support rental rate resilience and value creation; (3) experienced sponsors with clear business plans attract lender interest, suggesting the window for acquisition and light-touch renovations remains open despite higher interest-rate environment; (4) the Upper West Side and similar constrained neighborhoods remain prime for small-cap development or repositioning rather than new ground-up construction.

stories.title: National City Investment Group Commences Workforce Housing Build
stories.excerpt: The National City Investment Group, a locally owned, privately held real estate investment company, recently broke ground on Market View, a 120-unit multifamily residential community located at 303 Highland Ave. in National City. The development will transform an underutilized parking lot adjacent to Manolo Farmers Market, which has served National City for more than 33 years, into a residential community. Market View is scheduled for completion in the first quarter of 2028. “By bringing much-needed housing to National City, the National City Investment Group is helping create a more vibrant, walkable community that supports local businesses, and contributes to the continued revitalization of the area,” said Paul Najar, EVP, Gafcon PM-CM LLC, which is providing real estate advisory and project management services for the development. Designed by RDC with R.D. Olson Construction serving as the general contractor and McCullough Landscape Architecture handling landscape design, Market View will offer workforce housing in three distinct residential buildings linked by open space, pedestrian connectivity and Manolo Farmers Market. The post National City Investment Group Commences Workforce Housing Build appeared first on Connect CRE.

stories.summary: National City Investment Group commenced construction on Market View, a 120-unit workforce housing community in National City, California, scheduled to open in Q1 2028. The development transforms an underutilized parking lot at 303 Highland Avenue adjacent to the long-established Manolo Farmers Market into three residential buildings connected by open space and pedestrian walkways. The project is designed to support local business revitalization and community walkability in the area.
stories.impact: Ground-break on workforce housing in National City (south San Diego County submarket) signals continued demand for workforce/attainable-rate rentals and investor confidence in secondary San Diego submarkets. The focus on adaptive reuse of parking lots and community integration (farmers market co-tenancy, walkability) reflects regulatory and market pressure toward mixed-use, transit-oriented infill. For developers in San Diego County and Southwest U.S. metros, this validates: (1) workforce housing remains fundable and achieves near-term lease-up; (2) co-location with community anchors (retail, markets) enhances project viability and local support; (3) completion lag (Q1 2028 start-to-finish) suggests construction cost and labor remain elevated, putting pressure on proforma yields on workforce units.

stories.title: Report: Seattle-Tacoma Area Office Market Sees Declining Vacancy
stories.excerpt: The Seattle-Tacoma metro area office is showing signs of declining vacancy, according to a recent report by Marcus & Millichap. “Seattle-Tacoma’s office market is showing broader signs of stabilization as improving absorption and a nearly empty development pipeline support declining vacancy, although recovery continues to vary by property class and submarket,” said Joel Deis, senior managing director, market leader. Key findings of the report include that approximately 2.8 million square feet of office space was absorbed on net during the year ended in June, lowering vacancy from a peak of 19.7% in the second quarter of 2025 to 18.6%. Development will be virtually nonexistent in 2026, with only two properties totaling 35,000 square feet scheduled for completion. The previously anticipated delivery of Amazon’s roughly 1 million-square-foot Bellevue 600 Tower 1 is no longer expected this year.The 2026 forecast calls for vacancy to decline 80 basis points to 18.4% and average asking rent to increase 0.8% to $29.30 per square foot by year-end, although downtown rents may continue to face downward pressure. The post Report: Seattle-Tacoma Area Office Market Sees Declining Vacancy appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Seattle-Tacoma office vacancy declined to 18.6% in June 2025 from 19.7% peak (Q2 2025); net 2.8M SF absorbed YoY
Development pipeline virtually empty: only 35,000 SF scheduled 2026; Amazon's Bellevue 600 Tower 1 (~1M SF) no longer expected this year
2026 forecast: vacancy declines 80 bps to 18.4%; asking rents increase 0.8%; stabilization underway despite uneven recovery by class/submarket
stories.summary: Seattle-Tacoma's office market is stabilizing, with vacancy declining to 18.6% in June 2025 from a peak of 19.7% in Q2 2025, driven by 2.8 million square feet of net absorption over the trailing year. The development pipeline is nearly empty, with only 35,000 square feet expected to deliver in 2026. Amazon's anticipated Bellevue 600 Tower 1 delivery (~1 million SF) has been pushed beyond 2026. Forecasts call for an additional 80-basis-point vacancy decline in 2026 and 0.8% rent growth.
stories.impact: Positive office absorption and minimal future supply signal pent-up demand recovery in Seattle-Tacoma, but Amazon's delayed tower completion dampens near-term job growth expectations. For multifamily developers: (1) office stabilization and modest rent growth do not yet signal robust renter in-migration; (2) the delay of Amazon's 1M SF Bellevue campus is a cautionary signal—it reduces anticipated high-income employment in the tech sector and suggests tech hiring remains uncertain, which weakens apartment demand assumptions in the Seattle-Bellevue submarket over the next 12–24 months; (3) builders should expect slower pace of household formation than pre-pandemic and underwrite to lower rent growth in Bellevue/East King County luxury segments dependent on tech worker in-migration.

stories.title: Shorenstein Signs 78K SF in Office Leases at Repositioned D.C. Building
stories.excerpt: Shorenstein announced Monday that it has secured approximately three office leases totaling 78,000 square feet at its recently repositioned building in Washington, D.C.’s East End. Policy analysis and consulting firm Capstone signed the largest lease at approximately 43,000 square feet. Government relations and lobbying firm Monument Advocacy signed for 25,000 square feet, and the nonprofit Skoll Foundation signed for 10,000 square feet, according to Avison Young, which represented Shorenstein. The brokerage did not disclose the lengths of the leases or the asking rents at the property. Shorenstein acquired the property at 901 K Street NW in June 2025 for $84.3 million, property records show, and spent the past year upgrading the building. Improvements include a renovated lobby, a new conference and event center, enhancements to the rooftop terrace and expanded tenant amenities. “The leasing momentum at 901 K Street is the result of the market’s continued flight to quality,” Avison Young’s Jonathan Wellborn said in a statement. Wellborn, Eli Barnes and Will Stern of Avison Young’s D.C. agency leasing team represented Shorenstein in the transactions. “Companies are investing in workplaces that help attract talent, strengthen culture and support collaboration,” Barnes said. “901 K Street delivers that experience through its prime location, upgraded amenities and vibrant retail offerings.” Shorenstein specializes in acquiring and repositioning office and mixed-use properties across major U.S. markets. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Shorenstein signed three office leases totaling 78,000 SF at 901 K St. NW, Washington, D.C.

stories.summary: Shorenstein announced leasing of approximately 78,000 square feet across three office tenants at its repositioned property, 901 K Street NW, in Washington, D.C.'s East End. The largest lease went to policy consulting firm Capstone (43,000 SF), followed by government relations firm Monument Advocacy (25,000 SF) and nonprofit Skoll Foundation (10,000 SF). Shorenstein acquired the property in June 2025 for $84.3 million and completed upgrades including a renovated lobby, new conference center, enhanced rooftop, and expanded amenities.
stories.impact: Successful leasing of 78,000 SF at repositioned D.C. office property signals continued flight-to-quality in Washington's office market and confidence in East End submarket revitalization. However, this is office-focused activity with limited direct relevance to multifamily development. Indirectly, the strong leasing of policy/lobbying/nonprofit tenant mix reflects stable government-sector employment and think-tank presence in D.C., which supports underlying workforce stability and rental demand for mid-to-upper-income renters in nearby neighborhoods. For multifamily developers in D.C., this validates that office-dependent employment (federal, lobbying, NGOs) remains resilient; however, conversion or demolition of office to residential is not yet widely occurring in D.C. proper—office supply and demand remain in balance at trophy properties, lowering immediate redevelopment pressure.

stories.title: Octagon Lends $48M on Missouri Office-to-Resi Conversion of Former 7Up HQ
stories.excerpt: A building that forged the rise of a soda brand in the 1960s and `70s is poised for a fizzy makeover with some fresh creative capital. A joint venture between Revive Capital Development and KAI Design + Build has secured $48.25 million of construction financing to facilitate an office-to-residential conversion of the former 7Up global headquarters in Clayton, Mo., Commercial Observer has learned. The financing package includes tax credits for historic rehabilitation. Octagon Finance provided the unitranche loan supporting the adaptive reuse of the 11-story building in Downtown Clayton 10 miles west of St. Louis into a 118-unit apartment complex. The 200,000 square-foot redevelopment project called the Upton will be built at the site where 7Up launched its Uncola campaign in 1968. Zach Bubrosky, head of originations for Octagon Finance, said adaptive reuse was an ideal solution for the former 7Up building given the historic nature of the property and the need for new housing options or young professionals in an area close to Washington University in St. Louis. The soda company relocated from Clayton to Dallas in the late `70s, and the building has been vacant for more than a decade. “When you’re doing these historic tax credit projects, you have to maintain the historic integrity of the building,” said Bubrosky, noting that the building will have pictures of various 7Up bottles. “It makes for an interesting project while also giving back to the community in a way by providing additional housing at a time when you know there’s such a lack of housing supply in this market.” Located at 121 South Meramec Avenue, the Upton will have a unit mix of studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom apartments. Resident amenities will include a fitness center, a heated outdoor spa, a dog wash, a game room and fire pits. The 200,000-square-foot, 11-story historic building will be redeveloped into workforce housing for young professionals, with financing structured to include historic rehabilitation tax credits.
stories.impact: Historic adaptive reuse financing and project economics signal: (1) construction financing remains available for office-to-residential conversions in secondary metros (St. Louis submarket), with tax-credit structuring improving feasibility; (2) the explicit focus on workforce housing for young professionals reflects developer confidence in Clayton/St. Louis rental demand and attraction of emerging talent; (3) conversion of 11-story 200K SF office to only 118 units (~1,700 SF/unit) suggests high-ceiling, low-density adaptive reuse typical of historic buildings—lower unit density reduces per-unit capital efficiency but strong tax-credit subsidy offsets; (4) this deal validates that off-market historic structures in declining office submarkets (Downtown Clayton) can be repositioned to meet workforce renter demand, particularly where local demand/population growth supports absorption; developers in secondary Midwest metros should scout similar historic office buildings where land-cost basis is low and tax credits are available.

stories.title: AI Firm Minerva Doubles Office Footprint at the Refinery at Domino
stories.excerpt: Two Trees Management has signed a deal with an artificial intelligence firm to more than double its office space on the Williamsburg, Brooklyn, waterfront, Commercial Observer has learned. Data platform Minerva BI, which stands for business intelligence, expanded from 3,500 square feet on the third floor of the Refinery at Domino to 8,320 square feet on the 10th floor of the new-ish development, according to tenant broker Cushman & Wakefield. Two Trees did not immediately disclose the length of the lease, but asking rent in the building ranges from $68 to $86 per square foot. “Minerva’s expansion at the Refinery reflects both the company’s impressive growth trajectory and the continued appeal of the building to like-minded innovative technology firms,” C&W’s Sam Hoffman, who represented the tenant, said in a statement. “There was significant interest from other expanding tenants within the building, so securing this space required us to move quickly and strategically. We were able to position Minerva ahead of competing demand and secure the additional space needed to support its next phase of growth.” Two Trees had in-house representation in the transaction. “It has been a pleasure to see Minerva expand its footprint at the Refinery and enter its next phase of growth,” Alyssa Zahler, managing director of commercial leasing for Two Trees, said in a statement. “Companies like Minerva are an important part of the innovative technology and AI community that makes the Refinery such a dynamic place to work.” Other tenants in the revitalized Brooklyn sugar factory include event space operator Skylight, which expanded to 13,600 square feet in May, and AI-driven marketing support platform Mega, which signed a 3,926-square-foot lease in December 2025. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Minerva BI (AI/data platform firm) expanded office footprint at Refinery at Domino, Williamsburg, Brooklyn, from 3,500 to 8,320 SF

stories.summary: Data platform firm Minerva BI more than doubled its office space at Two Trees Management's Refinery at Domino, a mixed-use development on the Williamsburg, Brooklyn waterfront, expanding from 3,500 square feet to 8,320 square feet on the 10th floor. Asking rent in the building ranges from $68 to $86 per square foot. Two Trees reported significant competing interest from other expanding technology tenants, signaling strong demand for office space at the property.
stories.impact: High competition for space and Minerva's rapid expansion reflect sustained demand for creative office and tech-tenant tenancy in Brooklyn waterfront markets, but this is office-focused activity. Indirectly, strong office leasing velocity at mixed-use Refinery at Domino (owned by Two Trees, a major residential developer) underscores that Williamsburg remains a magnet for young tech workers and VC-backed AI/data firms—a proxy for high-income renter in-migration. For multifamily developers in Williamsburg and North Brooklyn: (1) the co-tenancy of office tech firms in mixed-use properties signals potential for residential units in the same buildings to command premium rents; (2) Minerva's expansion validates continued job-creation in AI/data sectors in NYC, supporting rental demand for 25–35-year-old earners; (3) Two Trees' ability to lease competing space quickly suggests Williamsburg remains undersupplied for tech-office space, which may boost residential demand and rent growth in nearby apartments targeting same demographic.

Approximately 80 percent of the existing occupants have operated at the center for more than a decade. Supermarket chain Ralphs, which has anchored the property since its opening with 44,000 square feet, or about 37 percent of its leasable space. Other tenants include Jersey Mike’s Subs, The UPS Store, Cold Stone Creamery, WaBa Grill, Chase Bank, Carl’s Jr., Carbon Health, Phenix Salon Suites and Australian Swim School. “The center serves a dense trade area with strong household incomes and limited new retail supply,” CBRE’s Mark Damiani said in a statement. “More than 147,000 people live within three miles of the center, and nearby new housing continues to add to the demand that Ralphs and the surrounding tenants serve.” The surrounding five-mile trade area contains more than 372,700 residents, with an average household income of approximately $154,800, according to CBRE.
